newsitem.title: UK: UK govt says still pressing on post-Barings laws.
newsitem.headline: UK govt says still pressing on post-Barings laws.

text.p: The British government is still pressing for progress on legislation prompted by the collapse of Barings Bank, it said in a statement on Thursday.

"The Treasury and UK supervisors are contributing actively to achieving maximum progress on the lead regulator intiative proposed by the Prime Minister and Chancellor and adopted by the G7 summit at Lyon in June 1996," it said in a response to a Treasury Select Committee report on post-Barings legislation.
"This work includes examination of legal barriers to effective supervisory cooperation," the government statement said.

At the Lyon summit, finance ministers from the seven largest industrialised nations called called for enhanced cooperation across international financial markets to strengthen the supervision of financial institutions.
Britain put forward the idea of a "convening regulator" to take the lead in responding to a fast-breaking financial crisis spanning the globe.
Barings collapsed ignominiously two years ago when Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson ran up debts of almost $1.4 billion in unauthorised derivatives trades.
Dutch banking giant ING eventually stepped in to buy the stricken bank -- which was Britain's oldest merchant bank.

The government said it would continue to argue for improvements to information exchanges across national boundaries and ensure that British legislation is kept up to date and corresponds with international obligations.

It said there were arguments in favour of the Treasury taking ministerial responsibility for all aspects of financial regulation. "But the recommendation raises wider issues which will need careful consideration before decisions are taken."
